opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple observation about where intelligence actually comes from. If you look at how humans or animals learn, we don't start from text. A baby learns about gravity, about objects persisting when they're hidden, about cause and effect, long before it learns a single word. That understanding comes from continuous streams of vision, touch, sound, and movement. Language is something we layer on top of that grounding, not the foundation itself.

Large language models have shown us something remarkable: if you compress enough of human writing, you get surprisingly general capabilities. But text is already a very abstracted, filtered description of the world. Someone has looked at reality, decided what matters, and written it down. When you train only on that, you inherit both the richness and the blind spots of language. Things like how a cup actually tips over, how much force you need to open a drawer, how light changes when you move your head. These are rarely written down, because to humans they're too obvious to describe.

So when we started Lingbo, the question we kept coming back to was: if we want systems that can really operate in the physical world, whether that's robots, autonomous vehicles, or interactive world models, shouldn't they learn the way the physical world presents itself? Through pixels over time, through depth, through sensor signals, through the consequences of actions. Video is especially important here because it carries time. It encodes dynamics, causality, physics, all implicitly. It's the closest thing we have at scale to raw experience.

There's also a practical side. My background is in generative models and visual representation, and over the past few years we've seen video generation go from blurry clips to things that look strikingly real. But looking real and being physically consistent are different things. A generated video can be beautiful and still have objects pass through each other. That gap told us the models were learning appearance more than understanding. To close it, you have to build the learning process around physical signals natively, not treat vision as an add-on adapter to a language model.

And honestly, I think the data argument is compelling too. Text on the internet is finite, and we're getting close to using most of the high-quality portion. The physical world, by contrast, generates an essentially unlimited stream of information every second, from cameras, from cars, from robots. If we can learn efficiently from that, the ceiling is much higher.

So it wasn't a contrarian bet for its own sake. It was more a conviction that the next step in AI has to be grounded in reality, and the most honest way to get there is to let the model see and interact with the world directly, rather than only reading about it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from real-world sensors and physical signals, but it does not identify a mismatch between clean academic datasets and unavoidable sensor noise in real-world robot operation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started with a frustration rather than a grand vision.

When we were working on video generation, we kept hitting the same wall. The models could produce clips that looked stunning for a few seconds, but the moment you asked them to do something that required actually understanding the world, like a cup tipping over, water pouring, a hand grasping something at the right angle, they would fall apart. Not because they lacked data, but because the data they learned from was already flattened. It was text describing the world, or images that had been curated and captioned by people. Everything was mediated through human language first.

And I kept thinking: a child doesn't learn physics from captions. A child learns by watching things fall, by touching, by seeing the same object from a hundred angles across a day. The raw signal is continuous, multimodal, and full of structure that we never bother to write down because it's too obvious to put into words. Gravity, occlusion, friction, how light behaves. Nobody writes a caption saying "the shadow moved because the object moved." But a sensor sees that every frame.

So the decision with Lingbo was really a bet that the cheapest and richest source of world knowledge is not the internet's text, it's the physical world itself, streaming in through cameras, depth sensors, IMUs, whatever you can attach. If you commit to learning from that natively, without translating everything into tokens that a language model happens to understand, you keep the information that language throws away.

There was also a practical side. If you want models that eventually act in the world, robotics, embodied agents, the representation has to be grounded in the same signals those systems will receive at deployment. Otherwise you're always building a bridge between two mismatched worlds, and the bridge is where things break.

It was a scarier path, because there's much less infrastructure and no obvious benchmark to chase. But I'd rather be early on the right path than optimized on the wrong one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language-mediated data with raw physical-world signals, but does not identify a mismatch between clean academic datasets and unavoidable sensor noise in real-world robotics.

astra-6.text:
For me, the starting point was a question: if we want intelligence to operate in the physical world, what should it learn from? Language can describe what happens, but it leaves out so much—the motion, the timing, the contact between objects, and how a situation changes as you act.

That’s what drew us toward real sensors and video at Lingbo. We wanted the physical world itself to provide the learning signal. Video captures how things unfold over time, and sensors can connect those observations to what a system actually experiences.

The ambition is to learn representations that help a system anticipate what happens next and adjust when reality differs from its prediction. I see that connection between perception, prediction, and action as central to building intelligence that can work in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from real sensors and video, but it does not identify the contrast between clean academic datasets and unavoidable sensor noise faced by real-world robots.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with a simple question: if we want AI to operate in the physical world, what should it learn from? Language gives us a powerful description of the world, but a description leaves things out. A video shows how objects move, how an action changes a scene, and how events unfold over time. Sensors give us another connection to what is actually happening.

That’s the motivation behind this direction for Lingbo. We want models to learn from observation and interaction, so their understanding is grounded in physical consequences. If something moves, what caused it? If I take an action, what might happen next? And when reality differs from my prediction, how do I update?

Language still matters—it helps us communicate goals and share knowledge. But I see it as part of that system. The commitment is to make physical experience central to learning, because that is the world we ultimately want the intelligence to understand and work in.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sensors and grounding models in physical experience, but it does not identify a contrast between clean academic datasets and unavoidable sensor noise for real-world robots.
